prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels, bringing frequency standards to the 1e-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep B042, Katori and Ye, as my final position, and the first-round exchange has made me more rather than less confident in it. My own opening first choice was B057, and I still think the Higgs observation is the most important physics on the list, but the discussion has shown that the obstacle is not the physics, it is whether three founding leaders can honestly stand for the discovery. The committee's task, as I understand it, is to identify the discovery and then the people behind it, and for the lattice clock the second step has a direct answer: Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice that cancels the light shift and for the first demonstrations, Ye for taking strontium lattice clocks to the 1e-18 regime and using them for redshift and fundamental-constant tests. The result has been reproduced and compared by independent laboratories, so maturity is not in doubt. In answer to the chair's wording question, I think the citation can and must be built around the lattice trapping at the magic wavelength and the resulting accuracy and stability, with no reference to frequency metrology or optical clocks in general. That wording is what keeps the award separable from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and it claims no more than the two named people did.
statement.case_against: The objection I cannot fully remove is priority and breadth of credit. Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and other lattice-clock groups are outside the two names, and nobody in this committee, including me, has checked the early-proposal and first-demonstration record in detail. As a theorist I am not the right person to settle it, and I do not want my support to be read as a claim that the two-name attribution is airtight. A second weakness is that Ye's accuracy work relies on comb and ultrastable-laser technology honoured in 2005, so the novelty rests mostly on Katori's concept and its realisation; Mehlig is right that the balance between the two names is less even than it first looks. For B057, my reservation is unchanged: a prize to Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee would honour founding and leadership of two experiments, the committee has not adopted a convention for large collaborations, and I do not think we should settle that policy question inside a single prize that also needs a precise citation.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B033 (dynamical mean-field theory) and ranks B042 only as an alternative, citing overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, the unreached redefinition of the second, and unresolved contributors.
responses.response: I take his novelty objection seriously, but I think it conflates the enabling toolbox with the invention. The comb supplied a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize honoured control of single ions; the distinctive step of the lattice clock, many neutral atoms held with the light shift engineered away, was part of neither, and Olsson and Pearce make the same point. On timing, the physics at the 1e-18 level is confirmed by independent laboratories, and the redefinition of the second is a metrological decision that does not change what was discovered. I accept that his own B033 is mature and influential, but by his own account the credit would leave out Metzner and the first step, and the method-versus-discovery question is open, so I cannot move it into the preferred configuration. I read this as a disagreement about the kind of achievement, not a verdict on DMFT.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B019 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene) as a young platform with a quantitative prediction followed by experiment, and says B042 is his fallback, adding that Ye's accuracy work leans heavily on comb technology.
responses.response: His comb remark is correct and I have changed the citation because of it, since it now rests on the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation rather than on precision measurement generally. I agree that the prediction-then-experiment structure of B019 is unusually attractive and that the criterion is a discovery, not a closed theory of its origin. Where I differ is timing: the pairing mechanism, the dependence on twist angle and sample quality, and the omission of the junior experimentalists who made the first measurements all say the picture is still moving. I do not think waiting a few years costs us much, and I keep B019 as my second alternative. Since he already names B042 as his fallback, I think we are less far apart than the first ranking suggests.

responses.point: Kroll was asked by the chair whether interrogating many atoms simultaneously is the decisive point of separation, and he argued that the magic-wavelength scheme removes the light shift and is distinct from the 2005 comb work.
responses.response: I defer to him on the spectroscopy, but his own account supplies the wording I need: the decisive novelty is trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, so that the light shift vanishes and Doppler and recoil effects are suppressed, and this brings the stability and accuracy near 1e-18. I have placed that in the citation. I would ask him to say whether the stability gain from many atoms is separable from what the 2012 ion clocks achieved, because that is the answer to the novelty objection that I, as a non-specialist, cannot supply from my own knowledge.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranks B042 first and B057 as his first alternative, and says he would not resist B057 if the committee adopted a convention for crediting large collaborations.
responses.response: I agree that the choice between B042 and B057 turns on that convention and not on the science, and I appreciate that he would not make B057 the lead on the present attribution. My answer to the chair's question is that the committee has not adopted such a convention in this exchange, and that a citation honouring detector concepts and leadership would have to say so openly, which is a coherent prize but a different one from a prize for the discovery. I would therefore keep B057 as my first alternative and be ready to reconsider if the committee settles the policy. I also agree with him that the citation must be written narrowly around the lattice scheme.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the early-proposal record be checked so that Katori is credited for the right step and the citation does not over-reach, and she distinguishes the comb as a ruler from the lattice clock as a way to hold many atoms with the perturbation engineered away.
responses.response: I agree and I share her uncertainty: none of us has verified the record, and I do not want to claim a priority I cannot document. I have tried to phrase the citation as the invention and realisation of the lattice clock, so that it describes the scheme and its demonstrated performance without asserting who was first for every sub-step. If the committee finds that another group has a documented claim to the proposal or first demonstration, I would want that to be raised before the vote and not after.

uncertainties: Whether the early-proposal and first-demonstration record supports crediting only Katori and Ye, or whether Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto or others hold priority claims that a two-name credit cannot accommodate; I cannot verify this from the supplied material.

Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice scheme is separable from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser contribution can be kept out of the citation.
Whether the committee will adopt a convention for crediting large collaborations, which alone would change my ranking of B057.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay recognition, a view I do not hold but cannot exclude among colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist; my recorded ties (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) lie in string theory and cosmology. I am a theorist and not an expert in atomic clocks or detector collaborations, so I rely on Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce for the metrological and experimental detail. I note the disclosures of Olsson on Japanese institutions in relation to B042 and take them as procedural flags that need no change to my own position.
